teaser: Yards of green silk, and a quiet argument about who really runs France.
review_notes:
Boucher named inspector at the Gobelins in 1755 and lodged in the Louvre from 1752: check dates.
Pompadour named lady-in-waiting (dame du palais) to the queen in February 1756: check.
Painting shown at the Salon of 1757; size about 201 x 157 cm: check.
Ownership: HypoVereinsbank collection on long-term loan to the Alte Pinakothek since 1971: check.
The dog is usually identified as her spaniel Mimi: check.
The objects on the floor are read as engraving and drawing tools; in this image they are small.

lesson.text: In 1756 François Boucher was 53 and had every reason to feel safe. He had rooms in the Louvre, a fresh appointment as inspector of the royal Gobelins tapestry works, and more orders than his hand could fill. Nearly all of it hung on one person: the woman in the green dress.

She was born Jeanne-Antoinette Poisson, daughter of a financier, with no title at all. In 1745 she became the official mistress of King Louis XV and received the name Marquise de Pompadour. She took drawing lessons from Boucher, bought his pictures by the dozen, and had her brother put in charge of royal building works.

By 1756 her position had changed in a way the court whispered about. She was 34 and no longer shared the king's bed. She had become something harder to name and harder to dismiss: his closest friend and adviser. That year she was even made lady-in-waiting to the queen. She needed a new image. Boucher got the job.

lesson.title: Reading the pose
lesson.text: The picture is about 2 meters tall (6.5 feet). She is shown nearly life size, and every choice says “interrupted, not posing”.

spots.title: The glance away
spots.text: She looks off to the side, toward someone we cannot see. Rouge on the cheeks, powdered hair with a few flowers, a ribbon at the neck. Calm, awake, unbothered.

spots.title: The book
spots.text: An open book rests in her hand, a finger keeping the page. She was reading when the visitor arrived and intends to go on.

spots.title: The ladder of bows
spots.text: Pink ribbon bows run down the bodice, largest at the top. The French called this a ladder. Against the sea-green silk the pink does all the talking.

lesson.text: A reader, then, rather than a seductress. The pose borrows from portraits of learned men in their studies, and that was the message for a court that sneered at her birth. She had real grounds for it: she protected the authors of the great Encyclopédie and owned a library of several thousand volumes.

She did more than collect. Pompadour learned to etch, which means drawing on a copper plate with acid so it can be printed, and she published a set of her own prints. Boucher supplied many of the designs.
So where is she sitting? You might think you are looking at a wall with a bookcase and a gilded clock. Check the right side of the picture, just behind her shoulder, before you decide.
The back of her head appears a second time in the painting. Where?

spots.title: The reflection
spots.text: Her gray chignon, seen from behind. The whole background is a huge mirror in a gilded frame. The bookcase and the clock stand on our side of the room, behind us.

lesson.text: That mirror changes the picture. The books and the clock are reflections, so her library is where we stand: the viewer is placed among her books. And the gold curtains to either side pull back like those of a theater. Boucher designed stage sets for the Paris Opera, and it shows.

The king's mistress was also the best friend porcelain ever had in France. She pushed the royal factory to move to Sèvres, near her own château, and a deep pink used there was later nicknamed “rose Pompadour”.

Nothing here is painted from a quick sitting. The satin is built up with long, wet strokes of pale green over darker green, so the folds seem to crackle. Rococo is the name for this taste of the mid 1700s: curves, pastel colors, pleasure in surfaces. Boucher was its star.
A state portrait without a throne: Boucher uses books, letters and a mirror, not crowns, to say that this woman holds power.

With this much fabric, the picture could have collapsed into a heap of ruffles. It holds together because the silk, the furniture and the clutter follow a simple plan that you can trace with a finger.
Three lines organize all that silk.

lines.label: The long slope
lines.text: From her face, down the skirt, to the far left corner: one great diagonal. It makes her seem to recline and to tower over us at once.

lines.label: Head to desk
lines.text: A short, steep line runs from her head along her resting arm to the writing table. Mind and correspondence are connected.

lines.label: The floor
lines.text: Along the bottom runs a trail of things dropped on the parquet: dog, roses, tools, books. Her interests are spread out like evidence.

lesson.text: That trail on the floor is the part people skip. It is a list of what she does all day. And the little writing table beside her elbow, its drawer left open, holds the most serious items of all.
The portrait was shown to the Paris public at the Salon of 1757, the official exhibition held in the Louvre. Anyone could walk in and see how the most powerful commoner in France wished to be seen.

spots.title: Quill and drawer
spots.text: A quill stands in the inkwell of the open drawer, the key still in the lock. She has just been writing.

spots.title: The sealed letter
spots.text: A folded letter, a stick of red sealing wax, a candle to melt it. Her notes went to ministers and generals.

spots.title: The spaniel
spots.text: A small black and tan spaniel sits up and watches her. In portraits a dog stands for loyalty: here, hers to the king.

spots.title: Roses and tools
spots.text: Two cut roses beside slender drawing and engraving tools. The amateur artist has left her work on the floor.

spots.title: Prints and scrolls
spots.text: Sheets of prints and rolled papers spill from a portfolio. They point to her taste for drawing and her interest in maps and building plans.

spots.title: Red bindings
spots.text: Large books bound in red leather stamped with gold lie under the table. More reading, casually stacked.

spots.title: The clock
spots.text: A gilded clock with a plump child lounging beside it, reflected in the mirror. Time is passing, which a woman of 34 at this court knew well.

spots.title: The slippers
spots.text: Pink backless slippers peek out from under the hem: the one hint that this office is also a private room.

quiz.question: What was Madame de Pompadour's position in 1756?
options: The king's friend and adviser, and lady-in-waiting to the queen
A painter at the Gobelins works
quiz.explanation: She had stopped being his lover but remained his closest adviser.

quiz.question: What does the background of the portrait turn out to be?
quiz.explanation: The back of her head is reflected in it.

quiz.question: Which art did Pompadour practice herself?
quiz.explanation: She etched and published a set of her own prints.

quiz.question: What does Rococo mean?
options: A mid-1700s taste for curves, pastel colors and rich surfaces
quiz.explanation: Boucher was the leading Rococo painter.

quiz.question: What do the quill, sealing wax and letter suggest?
options: That she is writing a novel
That she takes part in the business of state
quiz.explanation: Her letters went to ministers and generals.

facts.text: Madame de Pompadour was born into the high nobility.
facts.explanation: She was born Jeanne-Antoinette Poisson, a financier's daughter with no title.

facts.text: Boucher designed stage sets as well as paintings.
facts.explanation: He worked for the Paris Opera, and the curtains in this portrait recall a stage.

facts.text: The bookcase in the portrait is a reflection.
facts.explanation: The whole background is a mirror, so the books stand on the viewer's side of the room.
